name: Nuer
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 8 other works consulted do not discuss stress. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Westermann 1912.
catalog_citation: Westermann, Diedrich. 1912. The Nuer Language. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin XV, Abt. III (Afrikanische Studien): 84-141. Berlin. Quoted from the author's Sonderabdruck (own pagination), Rosetta Project scan of the phonology part (archive.org).
catalog_locator: Sonderabdruck p. 10, §39 'Intonation' (p. 7 of the Rosetta Project 'phonology' extract, archive.org; journal pagination c. p. 93). Read; the scan's is garbled.
catalog_quote: The language has etymological tones, that is each syllable or word has its own tone, by which it is distinguished from other words which have the same sounds, but are of different meaning, as for instance:—kót God, kòt reed. But in most words these tones are distinctly heard only when the word is spoken separately; in connection with other words the tones are frequently changed. Besides the etymological tone there is a grammatical tone, certain categories of the grammar having their own tones, as for instance all personal pronouns have high tone, the verb in the past and passive has high-low tone. In the course of speech neighbouring tones unite by means of assimilation and dissimilation (contrast) into groups of tones; this may be called the rhythmical intonation. The stress tone lies on the stem-syllable. This is best observable in the plural of substantives, where the stem-syllable has a clearly distinguishable stress, as opposed to the pre- and suffixes.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (Rosetta Project extract of Westermann 1912, archive.org rosettaproject_nus_phon-1, 8 pp.). PDF page 7 = offprint p. 10, header 'WESTERMANN: The Nuer Language.', margin-numbered secs 34-39, heading 'Intonation.' before sec. 39. I rendered the page at 300 dpi and read the image directly (the scanned layer is garbled: 'stem-svllabh. 1 his'). The image reads, word for word as quoted: 'Besides the etymological tone there is a grammatical tone, certain categories of the grammar having their own tones, as for instance all personal pronouns have high tone, the verb in the past and passive has high-low tone. In the course of speech neighbouring tones unite by means of assimilation and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nuer is a tone language (lexical and grammatical tone); in addition, word stress falls on the stem (root) syllable, with prefixes and suffixes unstressed. Since native roots are monosyllabic (Reid 2019: 52-55), this amounts to root-syllable stress in polysyllabic (affixed) words.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is illustrated only by noun plurals with plural prefix ka-/ke- and suffixes. Elsewhere (grammar part) an emphatic negative particle is said to carry high tone 'and at the same time a stress'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (stem vs. affixes), in a section otherwise about tone; Westermann notes tones are clearest in words spoken in isolation. Data from Jikany (Eastern Nuer, Sobat), Gawar/Lau (Bahr el Zeraf) and White Nile speakers, 1910-1911. Modern primary descriptions (Reid 2019, Monich 2020, Gjersøe 2020) analyse Nuer purely in terms of tone (H/M/L), vowel length and phonation and make no statement about stress; Gjersøe 2020: 4 reports that Storch 2005 additionally claims Nuer has stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann 1912 describes Nuer from Jikany speakers near Nasir on the Sobat (Eastern Nuer/Jikany), a Gawar (Lau) woman from the Bahr el Zeraf, and men from the White Nile region (Western Nuer); he treats it as one language with few dialect differences. Modern sources examined: Reid 2019 = Lou Nuer (Eastern), Monich 2020 = mainly Bentiu (Western Nuer), Frank 1999 = Eastern Jikany (Nasir). All fall under nuer1246; Glottolog dialect codes not assigned here.

tone_statements.citation: Monich, Irina. 2026. Deictic tone in Nuer: a preliminary report. The University of Nairobi Journal of Language and Linguistics 12: 59-75. doi:10.66563/uonjll.v12i.3351.
tone_statements.quote: Nuer is a tonal language, with five surface tones (Monich 2020, 2023b; Reid 2019; Gjersøe 2019). Following Monich’s analysis (2020, 2023b), these surface tones represent three underlying tonemes: Low (v̀), High, and Rising. The High toneme has two allotones: a level high (v́) when occurring on breathy vowels, and a falling (v̂) tone when on modal vowels. Besides its basic rising allotone (v̌), the Rising toneme also has the following contextual variants: mid (v̄), low (v̀), and falling (v̂).
tone_statements.locator: p. 60, Section 2 'Basics of Nuer morphophonology'; TBU statement p. 61
tone_statements.summary: 3 underlying tonemes Low, High, Rising (Rising = LH), 5 surface tones; TBU mora, max 2 per syllable; floating distal H, moraic prefix, downstepped H; many affix tones polar. Nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Reid, Tatiana & Bert Remijsen. 2025. Nuer has a floating suprasegmental component consisting of quantity and tone. Phonology 42: e4. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0952675724000198.
tone_statements.quote: Nuer is a tonal language. Lou Nuer has three tonemes: High, Mid and Low. The tonemes have a variety of surface realisations including a rise and a fall (Gjersøe 2019; Reid 2019: 132–140, Reid 2024; Monich 2020). ... In summary, we hypothesise that the FSC consists of a floating mora and a High tone. The FSC is manifested in the surface phonology only when there is a preceding context
tone_statements.locator: p. 4, sec. 1.2; second part p. 9, end of sec. 2
tone_statements.summary: Three level tonemes H, M, L; rise and fall are surface realisations (H falls on modal vowels). Some nouns carry a floating mora + floating H at their left edge; f0/duration study, 8 speakers.

tone_statements.citation: Gjersøe, Siri & Bert Remijsen. 2024. Perceptual sensitivity to tonal alignment in Nuer. Language and Speech 67(1): 95-112 (first online 25 April 2023). doi:10.1177/00238309231162299. Open access (CC-BY); PMC10916342.
tone_statements.quote: ... with independent contrasts of vowel length, voice quality, and tone. ... As for tone, the inventory varies between dialects. In the Ethiopian variant, the main dialect under investigation here, there is a contrast in underlying specification between H(igh), L(ow), and toneless syllables. The H toneme is realized as a Fall (HL) when the syllable it is associated with has a modal-voiced vowel (cf. Monich, 2020). In the transcriptions and elsewhere in this paper, we are referring to tone in terms of the surface-phonological specification.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.2 'Nuer language situation and phonology' (page not recoverable from the XML; article pp. 95-112)
tone_statements.summary: Ethiopian (Gajaak) Nuer: underlying H vs L vs toneless syllables; H surfaces as Fall (HL) on modal vowels. F0/perception study of L vs HL fall timing; inventory said to vary by dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Reid, Tatiana. 2024. Nuer. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 54(1): 479-514 (Illustrations of the IPA; published online 20 November 2023). Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0025100323000191.
tone_statements.quote: Tone Nuer is a tonal language. Word-level stress is not attested in Nuer. There are three tonemes in the South Sudanese Nuer dialects: High, Mid and Low (Reid 2019). The tonemes have a variety of phonetic realisations as a function of syllable properties. The realisation of the tonemes is primarily conditioned by the voice quality of the vowel and, to a lesser extent, by vowel length (Reid 2019; Monich 2020). With respect to voice quality, the realisation of the High and the Mid tonemes appears to serve as one of the perceptual cues of the phonation contrast.
tone_statements.locator: JIPA 54(1), section 'Tone' (following the vowel-length section, before 'Register expansion'; c. pp. 496-499 of 479-514), with footnote 9 and Figure 9
tone_statements.summary: Three tonemes H, M, L on the (mostly monosyllabic) root syllable, lexical and grammatical, with phonation-conditioned allotones (H falling on modal vowels, M rising on breathy vowels); explicitly no word-level stress.

tone_statements.citation: Gjersøe, Siri. 2023. Tonal polarity and inflection allomorphy in Nuer. Manuscript, lingbuzz/007082 (v1 January 2023, v2 November 2023).
tone_statements.quote: I propose three underlying tonal specifications for Ethiopian Jikany: /H/, /L/, and toneless /Ø/. These tones have many allophonic realizations, and their surface-phonological form is laid out in this section. ... The /H/ tone contrasts with the /L/ tone as the minimal pairs illustrate in the breathy-voiced nouns in (13) and the modal-voiced nouns in (14)–(15). I postulate the syllable as the TBU. ... In addition to the /H/ and /L/ tones, I postulate toneless syllables in Nuer.
tone_statements.summary: Underlying /H/ vs /L/ plus toneless syllables; mid, HL, LH are surface allotones conditioned by phonation and position; floating H in FSC nouns; final lowering only; F0 tracks in appendix.

tone_statements.citation: Monich, Irina. 2023. Interaction of phonation and tone in Nuer. Phonological Data and Analysis 5(6): 1-40. doi:10.3765/pda.v5art6.35.
tone_statements.quote: Monich (2020) offered empirical evidence that a Nuer syllable can be associated with one of the following three tonemes – High, Low, and Rising – but avoided making claims about their underlying makeup. There are only three contrastive tonemes on the surface, as the high and falling tones are in perfect complementary distribution. ... Alternatively, are there two underlying tonemes, H and HL, which neutralize on the surface? Based on the available information so far, the last possibility appears to be the correct one.
tone_statements.locator: p. 14, sec. 5 'The underlying tonal oppositions'; cf. p. 2 sec. 1 (five surface contours; Low, Rising, High tonemes) and p. 36 (four underlying contrasts)
tone_statements.summary: Three surface tonemes High, Low, Rising (five surface contours incl. mid, falling); argues four underlying melodies H, L, LH, HL, H/HL neutralized by phonation. Suffix tone polar; stress not treated.

tone_statements.citation: Monich, Irina. 2020. Nuer tonal inventory. Studies in African Linguistics 49(1): 1-42. doi:10.32473/sal.v49i1.122257.
tone_statements.quote: This article offers empirical evidence that the Nuer tonal system is comprised of three tonemes: Low, High and Rising. However, the Nuer syllable can be associated with one of five tonal contours: high, low, rising, falling and mid. We argue that the mid and rising tones are variants of the same toneme – which we call Rising ... Phonation of the tone-bearing vowel plays a crucial role in realization of the tonal contour: High toneme is pronounced with a flat high pitch over breathy vowels, but with a falling pitch over modal vowels.
tone_statements.locator: p. 1, section 1 'Nuer tonal system'; restated p. 3 sec 3.1 and p. 36 sec 6
tone_statements.summary: Three tonemes High, Low, Rising; five surface tones (high, low, rising, falling, mid) are allotones; High is falling on modal vowels; Rising = L+H autosegments. No downstep or stress discussed.

tone_statements.citation: Monich, Irina. 2017. Vowel length in Nuer. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 4 (AMP 2016). Linguistic Society of America. doi:10.3765/amp.v4i0.4006.
tone_statements.quote: Nuer is a tonal language. There are two lexically specified tones: H, L. An intriguing feature of the Nuer tonal system is that the H-tone over modal vowels is always realized as a fall.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2, sec. 2 'Basics of Nuer phonology', last paragraph
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical tones H and L; H on modal vowels surfaces as a fall. Tone also listed as one of four stem-modification parameters in noun inflection (p.1, p.3). Paper is about 3-way vowel length.

[...] Similar compensatory lengthening of vowels before occasionally eliding glides or vowels is still an ongoing process in Shilluk and Nuer (Reid 2009, 2019).
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: The survey lists Nuer among the stressless West Nilotic tone languages, with tone, vowel length and voice quality as independent syllable-level parameters and compensatory lengthening still active. The entry's tone-and-stress class rests on Westermann 1912's 'stress tone' on the stem syllable, which this statement (a consensus summary after Reid 2019 and others, not new data) denies.

sources.citation: Reid, Tatiana. 2024. Nuer. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 54(1): 479-514 (Illustrations of the IPA; published online 20 November 2023). Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0025100323000191.
sources.quote: Tone Nuer is a tonal language. Word-level stress is not attested in Nuer. There are three tonemes in the South Sudanese Nuer dialects: High, Mid and Low (Reid 2019). The tonemes have a variety of phonetic realisations as a function of syllable properties. The realisation of the tonemes is primarily conditioned by the voice quality of the vowel and, to a lesser extent, by vowel length (Reid 2019; Monich 2020). With respect to voice quality, the realisation of the High and the Mid tonemes appears to serve as one of the perceptual cues of the phonation contrast.

sources.citation: Gjersøe, Siri. 2023. Tonal polarity and inflection allomorphy in Nuer. Manuscript, lingbuzz/007082 (v1 January 2023, v2 November 2023).
sources.quote: I propose three underlying tonal specifications for Ethiopian Jikany: /H/, /L/, and toneless /Ø/. These tones have many allophonic realizations, and their surface-phonological form is laid out in this section. ... The /H/ tone contrasts with the /L/ tone as the minimal pairs illustrate in the breathy-voiced nouns in (13) and the modal-voiced nouns in (14)–(15). I postulate the syllable as the TBU. ... In addition to the /H/ and /L/ tones, I postulate toneless syllables in Nuer.
sources.note: Underlying /H/ vs /L/ plus toneless syllables; mid, HL, LH are surface allotones conditioned by phonation and position; floating H in FSC nouns; final lowering only; F0 tracks in appendix.

sources.citation: Monich, Irina. 2023. Interaction of phonation and tone in Nuer. Phonological Data and Analysis 5(6): 1-40. doi:10.3765/pda.v5art6.35.
sources.quote: Monich (2020) offered empirical evidence that a Nuer syllable can be associated with one of the following three tonemes – High, Low, and Rising – but avoided making claims about their underlying makeup. There are only three contrastive tonemes on the surface, as the high and falling tones are in perfect complementary distribution. ... Alternatively, are there two underlying tonemes, H and HL, which neutralize on the surface? Based on the available information so far, the last possibility appears to be the correct one.
sources.locator: p. 14, sec. 5 'The underlying tonal oppositions'; cf. p. 2 sec. 1 (five surface contours; Low, Rising, High tonemes) and p. 36 (four underlying contrasts)
sources.note: Three surface tonemes High, Low, Rising (five surface contours incl. mid, falling); argues four underlying melodies H, L, LH, HL, H/HL neutralized by phonation. Suffix tone polar; stress not treated.
sources.venue: Phonological Data and Analysis

sources.citation: Monich, Irina. 2017. Vowel length in Nuer. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 4 (AMP 2016). Linguistic Society of America. doi:10.3765/amp.v4i0.4006.
sources.quote: Nuer is a tonal language. There are two lexically specified tones: H, L. An intriguing feature of the Nuer tonal system is that the H-tone over modal vowels is always realized as a fall.
sources.locator: p. 2, sec. 2 'Basics of Nuer phonology', last paragraph
sources.note: Two lexical tones H and L; H on modal vowels surfaces as a fall. Tone also listed as one of four stem-modification parameters in noun inflection (p.1, p.3). Paper is about 3-way vowel length.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 4 (AMP 2016)
